name: Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis Type 1 (CLN1 Disease, PPT1 Deficiency)

clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1 (PPT1) due to biallelic CLN1 (PPT1) variants; a form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.
Classic phenotype is infantile-onset (Santavuori-Haltia): normal early development followed by rapid psychomotor regression, visual failure and seizures within the first years of life.
CLN1 is defined by the causative gene rather than age; later-onset late-infantile, juvenile and even adult presentations occur with the same enzyme defect.
Progressive microcephaly (acquired, deceleration of head growth) is characteristic of the infantile form, contrasting with several other storage disorders.
Myoclonus, ataxia, hand stereotypies and loss of acquired speech and motor skills are prominent as the disease advances.
Electron microscopy of tissue shows granular osmiophilic deposits (GRODs), the ultrastructural hallmark distinguishing CLN1 from the curvilinear and fingerprint profiles of other NCL subtypes.
Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating deficient PPT1 enzyme activity (readily measured in a dried blood spot or leucocytes) and by CLN1 molecular testing.
Management is supportive, focused on seizure control, spasticity, feeding, secretions and multidisciplinary palliative care; no approved disease-modifying therapy is established for CLN1.
reference.pathophysiology: CLN1 disease results from deficiency of palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1, a soluble lysosomal enzyme that removes palmitate (a thioester-linked fatty-acyl group) from cysteine residues of palmitoylated proteins, a step required for their normal lysosomal degradation and for recycling of the lipid modification. Loss of PPT1 activity impairs the turnover of S-acylated proteins and leads to lysosomal accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigment (ceroid and lipofuscin-like material) forming granular osmiophilic deposits within neurons and other cells. Neurons are exquisitely vulnerable: storage is accompanied by disrupted synaptic vesicle recycling, endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial stress, neuroinflammation with microglial and astrocytic activation, and progressive apoptotic neuronal loss, most strikingly in the cerebral and cerebellar cortex and the retina. The consequence is relentless grey-matter neurodegeneration producing regression, epilepsy, retinal degeneration with blindness and profound cerebral atrophy. The severity and age of onset broadly correlate with the amount of residual enzyme activity, explaining the spectrum from severe infantile to milder later-onset phenotypes carrying the same defect.
additionalDifferentials: Other neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, particularly CLN2 (TPP1 deficiency) and CLN3 (juvenile)
GM1 and GM2 gangliosidoses presenting with infantile regression
Rett syndrome (given hand stereotypies and regression in girls)
Mitochondrial encephalopathies with regression and epilepsy
Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome with acquired microcephaly and regression
additionalInvestigations: PPT1 enzyme activity assay in dried blood spot, leucocytes or fibroblasts (deficient)
Molecular genetic testing of the CLN1 (PPT1) gene
Electron microscopy of skin, conjunctiva or lymphocytes for granular osmiophilic deposits
MRI brain showing progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy with white-matter and thalamic signal change
Electroencephalography for epileptiform activity and progressive background attenuation
Electroretinography and ophthalmological assessment documenting retinal degeneration and optic atrophy
Serial head circumference measurement documenting acquired microcephaly in the infantile form
redFlags: Deceleration of head growth (acquired microcephaly) with developmental regression in an infant
New-onset myoclonus or drug-resistant seizures accompanying loss of skills
Progressive visual failure with retinal degeneration and optic atrophy
Rapid loss of previously acquired speech, motor and social milestones
Emergence of hand stereotypies and irritability with sleep disturbance
reference.prognosis: The classic infantile CLN1 phenotype is severe and rapidly progressive, leading to a vegetative state and death in childhood; later-onset forms progress more slowly but remain fatal neurodegenerative diseases.
pitfalls: Assuming CLN1 always presents in infancy and overlooking later-onset (juvenile or adult) presentations of the same PPT1 defect.
Misdiagnosing girls as Rett syndrome because of regression and hand stereotypies without measuring PPT1 activity.
Failing to request electron microscopy or enzyme testing when autofluorescent storage is suspected, delaying diagnosis.
Confusing CLN1 with CLN2, which has a distinct enzyme (TPP1), different ultrastructure and an available enzyme-replacement therapy.
Attributing acquired microcephaly to a primary structural or perinatal cause rather than a neurodegenerative storage process.
